qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Explain a reason for intervention where an invented workshop’s dust damages neighbouring gardens and the producer does not bear that damage cost.
items.canonical_answer: Neighbours experience an external cost not fully included in the producer’s decision. The firm may therefore produce more harmful activity than when that damage is considered; intervention can encourage prevention or make the cost relevant to its choices.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): harmful dust. Because/mechanism (2): third-party damage (1), absent from private cost (1). Consequence (1): reason to reduce unaccounted harm.
objective_titles: Explain the reasons for government’s intervention in business

items.prompt: Explain why a sealed-food buyer’s inability to observe contamination can support a role for product testing.
items.canonical_answer: The buyer lacks information needed to judge safety. Reliable testing can reveal hidden hazards and reduce exposure that ordinary price comparison cannot address.
marking_guidance: Context (1): hidden contamination. Reason/consequence (1): testing reduces relevant information gap.
objective_titles: Explain the reasons for government’s intervention in business

items.prompt: Explain how clear hygiene standards with competent inspection and effective correction can influence an invented food workshop’s production.
items.canonical_answer: The standard defines acceptable handling, inspection checks actual behaviour and correction makes breaches costly or requires improvement under the stated arrangement. The firm has reason to adopt safer production where monitoring and feasible compliance support the rule.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): standard introduced. Mechanism (2): inspection detects breaches (1), correction changes incentives/practice (1). Consequence (1): safer process conditional on enforcement and feasibility.
objective_titles: Explain how the government controls production of goods and services

items.prompt: Explain why a written production standard alone may leave an unsafe practice unchanged when nobody checks or follows up breaches.
items.canonical_answer: Without monitoring and correction, the producer may face little practical incentive to change. The written requirement does not itself establish effective compliance.
marking_guidance: Context (1): absent checking/follow-up. Reason/conclusion (1): formal rule insufficient to establish practice change.
objective_titles: Explain how the government controls production of goods and services

items.prompt: Evaluate inspection and accurate labelling for an invented sealed-food market where hazards are hidden, but inspection staff and testing funds are limited.
items.canonical_answer: Inspection can reveal hazards and labels can improve informed use. Limited staff/testing can miss problems and compliance uses resources. Support clear risk-focused checks and follow-up, with no blanket safety guarantee.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): identify relevant protection (1), explain reduced harm/unfairness (1). Argument against (2): supplied implementation limit (1), cost or access consequence (1). Condition (1): hidden hazards and accessible follow-up. Judgement (2): conditional recommendation (1), linked to mechanism and limit (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss how consumers are protected in Namibia

items.prompt: Evaluate a safety policy for an invented workshop with a missing machine guard, accessible confidential complaints and prompt inspection, but correction requires equipment expenditure.
items.canonical_answer: Protection can reveal and correct a serious hazard, reducing injury exposure. Equipment and enforcement cost resources, and reporting must remain trusted. Prompt effective correction is supported where the guard addresses the hazard; a written policy alone is insufficient.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): identify relevant protection (1), explain reduced harm/unfairness (1). Argument against (2): supplied implementation limit (1), cost or access consequence (1). Condition (1): trusted reporting and effective correction. Judgement (2): conditional recommendation (1), linked to mechanism and limit (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss how employees are protected by the State

items.prompt: Evaluate a workplace HIV and AIDS non-discrimination policy with education and confidential complaints, but limited awareness and concerns about unnecessary disclosure.
items.canonical_answer: Education can challenge status-based assumptions and a confidential complaint process can support fair review. Low awareness and disclosure fears can prevent access. Support a clearly communicated trusted process with appropriate privacy and follow-up; status alone does not establish inability to work.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): identify relevant protection (1), explain reduced harm/unfairness (1). Argument against (2): supplied implementation limit (1), cost or access consequence (1). Condition (1): awareness, privacy and fair follow-up. Judgement (2): conditional recommendation (1), linked to mechanism and limit (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss how the government can protect people with HIV and AIDS at the workplace

items.prompt: Define external cost (2). Identify two controls on harmful production (2). Explain how reliable testing can protect a consumer unable to see a sealed product’s hazard (2). Identify two employee interests relevant to State protection (2).
items.canonical_answer: An external cost is imposed on third parties and not fully reflected in the decision-maker’s private cost. Standards and inspection can control harmful activity. Testing reveals hidden hazards, supporting safer choices or correction. Safe work and fair treatment are employee interests.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): third-party cost (1), unaccounted in private decision (1). Separate points for controls (2): standard (1), inspection (1). Explanation (2): hidden hazard identified (1), exposure or information problem reduced (1). Identification (2): safety (1), fair treatment (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented Namibian food workshop: buyers cannot see a sealed-product hazard; workers report a missing machine guard and dust damaging neighbouring gardens. Product testing, clear labels, safety inspection and a confidential complaint route are proposed. A worker reports an employment decision based solely on perceived HIV status, not evidence of inability to perform the job. Limited inspectors and fear of unnecessary disclosure can impede follow-up. Describe three consumer/employee protection measures, each with a case detail (6). Explain the reasons for intervention using the external cost, information and vulnerability problems (7). Discuss the proposed consumer, employee and HIV-related protections given the implementation limits (7).
items.canonical_answer: Testing addresses hidden food hazards, labelling supports information and safety inspection addresses the missing guard. Garden damage is a third-party cost not borne in the workshop decision; buyers lack hazard information and workers may struggle to secure safe fair treatment alone. Protection can reduce harm and status-based unfairness, but limited inspection and disclosure fears weaken access. Support targeted checks and trusted confidential follow-up without assuming perfect compliance or inability from status.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): testing (1), hidden food hazard (1); labels (1), information need (1); safety inspection (1), missing guard (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): garden damage (1), third-party external cost (1), private decision omits it (1); buyer information gap (1), hidden product risk (1); worker vulnerability (1), reason for collective enforcement/protection (1). Both sides/judgement (7): safer goods (1), safer work (1), HIV non-discrimination/fair review (1); limited inspectors (1), disclosure fear (1); condition trusted effective follow-up (1); judgement combined targeted protection supported under that condition (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Invented same risks in two Namibian workshops: hidden product hazards, unsafe equipment and a complaint of discrimination based solely on perceived HIV status. Case 1 has competent inspection, timely correction, clear information and a trusted confidential complaint process. Case 2 has limited inspection capacity, delayed correction, low awareness and fear of unnecessary disclosure. The cases state implementation conditions, not actual findings about named businesses. Evaluate the protection approach in Case 1 for consumers, employees and workers affected by HIV-related discrimination (7). Evaluate whether the same written rules alone are sufficient in Case 2 (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1 combines hazard detection and correction with trusted fair review, supporting consumers and workers including people facing HIV-related discrimination. It still uses resources and cannot promise every breach is prevented. Case 2 retains a useful statement of expected behaviour but lacks effective access and enforcement. Prioritise feasible risk-focused checks, awareness and confidential follow-up; written rules alone are insufficient under those conditions.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for consumer safety (1), employee safety (1), HIV fair review/privacy (1); argument against resources/residual breaches (1); condition competent trusted follow-up (1); judgement effective approach supported (1), linked to implementation (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for clear rules (1), potential protection if applied (1); argument against inspection delays (1), awareness/disclosure barriers (1); condition access and enforcement improved (1); judgement written rules insufficient (1), targeted improvement tied to all affected groups (1). Total 14.
